commits.subject: Docs-as-code case study, stage 1: the help-center article as it stands
commits.body:
An original help-center article, in the shape of a Zendesk Guide API
record, about resetting a Keycloak user's second factor. It's the
starting point the next stages audit, restructure and migrate.

commits.subject: Docs-as-code case study, stage 2: audit the article
commits.body:
Fourteen findings, each with the quote, the problem and the fix. Two are
critical: the article's main step leaves the account with a password
alone (checked against the server's recorded behaviour), and nothing
asks the administrator to confirm who is asking. The audit also maps
the content to four pages: a concept, a how-to, a reference and a
troubleshooting page.

commits.subject: Docs-as-code case study, stage 3: a Docusaurus project for the docs
commits.body:
Docusaurus 3.10.2 in docs-only mode, one sidebar ordered by purpose
(concepts, how-to guides, reference, troubleshooting), two components
(a screenshot with its caption, and the page facts read from front
matter), and Vale with the Google, alex and Readability packages plus
house rules that come from the audit. English is the source locale;
qps-ploc is a pseudo-locale for testing translation readiness.

commits.subject: Docs-as-code case study, stage 4: migrate the article to MDX
commits.body:
The one article becomes five pages split by purpose: an overview, a
concept, a how-to, a reference for the OTP policy and the terminology,
and a troubleshooting page. Each page has front matter for its type,
audience, product version, owner and last review. The identity check is
one partial, reused by the how-to and the troubleshooting page. The
screenshots come from the Keycloak 26.8.2 server the steps were checked
on, with alternative text and captions.

The first build failed: YAML reads last_review as a Date, which React
can't render. PageFacts now shows it as an ISO 8601 date.

commits.subject: Docs-as-code case study, stage 5: lint with Vale and review the results
commits.body:
Vale 3.28.1 with Google, alex, Readability and the house rules, run on
the original article and on the migration. The migration went from 26
errors, 41 warnings and 99 suggestions to 0 errors, 8 warnings and 72
suggestions. Each accepted and rejected finding has its reason in
quality/decisions.md. Interface labels and Keycloak's own messages are
quoted, so they're out of scope; alex's warning on "period" is off.

Vale didn't catch the original article's two critical problems. The
audit did.

commits.subject: Docs-as-code case study, stage 6: pseudo-localize to test translation readiness
commits.body:
scripts/pseudo.mjs writes a qps-ploc copy of every page and of the
theme's strings: accented, about 35% longer and bracketed. It's a test,
not a translation, and the build says so on every page. Code, URLs,
link targets, heading IDs and image paths stay as they are.

The first pseudo-locale build found the one thing a translator couldn't
reach: the labels of PageFacts (Type, For, Checked against, Owner, Last
review) are hard-coded in English on every page.
scripts/check-pseudo.py lists them; quality/ keeps the run and its
screenshot. The next commit fixes it.

commits.subject: Docs-as-code case study, stage 6: make the page labels translatable
commits.body:
PageFacts's five labels are literal translate() calls, so
write-translations extracts them. A first attempt built the message ID
from a variable, and extraction refused it. The pseudo-locale build now
leaves no English in any page's content, and holds at 390 px. The
test banner is part of the page instead of sitting over it.
localization.md says what the source does for translators and how it
was tested.

commits.subject: Docs-as-code case study, stage 7: revise the how-to with a tested REST API method
commits.body:
Version 1.1 of the pages adds a way to reset many users at once with
Keycloak's admin REST API: after an OTP policy change, every user needs
a reset, and the console does one at a time. Every command ran as
written against Keycloak 26.8.2 (revision/evidence.json), and a sign-in
afterwards reached Mobile Authenticator Setup.

Testing the commands found a trap: a PUT of a user's required actions
replaces the whole list, so sending CONFIGURE_TOTP alone removed a
pending profile update. The guide now reads the list first and adds to
it, with a warning that says why.

Also: a Changes page, the review date corrected to 2026-11-27 on every
page, and code-block titles in the pseudo-locale, which the check found
still in English. Vale: 0 errors.

+## Reset many users with the admin REST API {#rest-api}
+
+After a change to the [OTP policy](../reference/otp-policy.mdx#before-change), every user's authenticator needs a reset, and the admin console does one user at a time.
+The admin REST API does the same two things: it deletes the OTP credential, and it adds **Configure OTP** to the user's required actions.
+
+<ConfirmIdentity />
+
+Set these variables first.
+Read the password from a password manager or a prompt, so that it stays out of your shell history.
+
+```bash title="Variables"
+KC_URL=https://keycloak.example.com   # your Keycloak server
+REALM=portfolio-demo                  # the user's realm
+KC_ADMIN=sam.rivera                   # an administrator of the master realm
+USERNAME=alex.morgan                  # the user to reset
+read -rs -p "Password for $KC_ADMIN: " KC_ADMIN_PASSWORD; echo
+```
+
+1. Get an access token for the admin REST API, and find the user's ID.
+
+   ```bash
+   TOKEN=$(curl -s "$KC_URL/realms/master/protocol/openid-connect/token" \
+     -d grant_type=password -d client_id=admin-cli \
+     --data-urlencode "username=$KC_ADMIN" --data-urlencode "password=$KC_ADMIN_PASSWORD" | jq -r .access_token)
+   USER_ID=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
+     "$KC_URL/admin/realms/$REALM/users?username=$USERNAME&exact=true" | jq -r '.[0].id')
+   ```
+
+2. Delete each of the user's OTP credentials.
+   Keycloak answers each deletion with `204 No Content`.
+
+   ```bash
+   for ID in $(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$KC_URL/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$USER_ID/credentials" \
+     | jq -r '.[] | select(.type == "otp") | .id'); do
+     curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
+       "$KC_URL/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$USER_ID/credentials/$ID"
+   done
+   ```
+
+3. Add `CONFIGURE_TOTP` to the user's required actions.
+
+   :::warning Keep the actions already there
+   A `PUT` replaces the user's whole list of required actions.
+   Sending `{"requiredActions": ["CONFIGURE_TOTP"]}` alone removes any action the user still has to do, such as updating their profile.
+   Read the list first and add to it, as this command does.
+   :::
+
+   ```bash
+   ACTIONS=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$KC_URL/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$USER_ID" \
+     | jq -c '.requiredActions + ["CONFIGURE_TOTP"] | unique')
+   curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
+     -d "{\"requiredActions\": $ACTIONS}" "$KC_URL/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$USER_ID"
+   ```
+
+4. Check the result.
+   The credentials list holds the password only, and the required actions include `CONFIGURE_TOTP`.
+
+   ```bash
+   curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$KC_URL/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$USER_ID/credentials" | jq -c '[.[] | .type]'
+   curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$KC_URL/admin/realms/$REALM/users/$USER_ID" | jq -c '.requiredActions'
+   ```
+
+   ```json title="Output"
+   ["password"]
+   ["CONFIGURE_TOTP","UPDATE_PROFILE"]
+   ```
+
+At their next sign-in, Keycloak runs the user's required actions one after another, and asks them to set up an authenticator before they get in.
+
 ## Next steps {#next-steps}
